prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the analysis of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: tractable time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts and policy rules, and the microfounded framework for evaluating policy

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) and treated B001 as the alternative because I weighted clean attribution above breadth. The exchange has narrowed the attribution problem and has also exposed the limits of my own first choice. B001 is a coherent set of originating ideas with separable roles. Calvo supplied the tractable time-dependent pricing device, Taylor the staggered-contract model and the policy rule, and Woodford the integrated microfounded and welfare-based framework for policy evaluation. The criterion that separates these three from Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is origin of the discovery rather than later estimation, canonisation or adoption. That criterion is not arbitrary, because the later work builds on the originating ideas and does not replace them. I did not apply it consistently in round 1. The core ideas are 25 to 45 years old. They have been extended through heterogeneous-agent and state-dependent pricing work. They are the benchmark used in the analysis of monetary policy, so the discovery has changed how a whole policy domain is reasoned about. The earlier macro prizes (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims, Phelps) covered expectations, time consistency and identification of policy effects. As Friberg notes, none covered pricing frictions, policy-rule analysis or the microfounded normative framework. The 2022 prize went to banks and financial crises, not to this core. This is a judgement about originality, durability and influence. It does not rest on the number of colleagues who list B001, and I do not count that as merit. My assessment rests on general knowledge and the supplied files, and I have not independently verified citation or adoption claims.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the main cost. A three-name cap excludes Galí and Gertler on the canonical New Keynesian model, Christiano and Eichenbaum on identified, estimated DSGE models, and Smets on central-bank adoption. Priority questions involving Fischer and Phelps are also unresolved, and Clarida is not on the ballot. Whether the Taylor rule is a scientific contribution or a policy prescription is an open question that the citation must handle, and I would put the weight on the rule as an analytical benchmark for policy. The empirical record is mixed: Phillips-curve fit, the role of heterogeneity, the evidence on state-dependent pricing, and the 2021-23 inflation. These limit the claim, and a committee that wants a framework prize resting on the estimated model could reach a different laureate set. A further point is that B002 has a cleaner two-person credit, and I still regard Kiyotaki-Moore as a foundational mechanism. I am moving it to an alternative because its stylisation, its mostly later-by-others empirical support and the neighbouring 2022 prize weigh more heavily on a first-place preference. I do not think those points make it a weak candidate.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first and holds that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are the origin points, while Galí, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum codified, estimated and extended the structure. He ranks B002 fifth as highly stylised, with mixed empirical quantification.
responses.response: In round 1 I accepted his reading of B002's stylisation but still ranked it first, treating stylisation as a strength of a foundational mechanism. I now give more weight to his second point: a prize for a mechanism that is largely backed by calibrated models is a narrower claim than one for an idea that organised a whole policy domain. His origin-point test is the criterion I lacked for B001, since it explains why the estimation-side contributors can be acknowledged without being credited here. I accept it, with the caveat that a committee that wanted to reward quantification would be rewarding a different discovery, and the citation should say which one it means. He is also a frequent co-author of mine, and I disclose that below.

responses.point: Friberg argues that the earlier macro prizes (Phelps, Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims) did not recognise pricing frictions, policy-rule analysis or the microfounded normative framework, and that B002 is partly covered by the 2022 prize whereas B001's core has no neighbouring recent award. He also notes that micro evidence shows state dependence that the Calvo device misses.
responses.response: I had cited the earlier prizes as narrowing the unclaimed ground on B001. His distinction answers that point: those prizes dealt with expectations, time consistency and identification, not with the pricing and rule structure central banks use. I accept it. On the 2022 overlap I still think it is smaller for B002 than some colleagues suggest, as I argued against Andersson in round 1, but it is not zero, and B001 faces nothing comparable. I agree with his state-dependence point. It limits the Calvo device as a literal description, and it is why the citation should say tractable time-dependent price setting as a benchmark. I also disclose our joint menu-costs work, which touches this topic.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first and B002 eighth. He raises whether the Taylor rule is science or policy prescription, the priority questions around Fischer and Phelps, and Gertler's overlap with both B001 and B002. He sees less unclaimed ground in B002.
responses.response: I partly disagreed with him on B002 in round 1 and still do on the size of the 2022 overlap, but his point about unclaimed ground is stronger now that the discussion has separated the cores. The trio also removes the Gertler problem he raised, since Gertler is credited in B002 but not in my proposed B001 laureate set. On the Taylor rule, I treat it as an analytical benchmark that made policy rules a subject of formal evaluation, and so as a scientific contribution as well as a practice. I accept that the committee must decide this explicitly. The Fischer and Phelps priority questions are not settled by the supplied evidence, and I list them as an uncertainty.

responses.point: Dreber shares my B002 first place but says our agreement should not count as merit. She asks whether the collateral-feedback mechanism has survived scrutiny and grants that its empirical support is suggestive, not settled. She also doubts that B002 can reach six votes.
responses.response: I agree that shared first-place rankings are not evidence, and I would add that my own B002 ranking is no evidence for it either. Her question is the right test. I can point to later work on housing collateral and firm investment that uses the mechanism, but I have not verified how strongly it supports quantitative importance, and I should not claim more than that. Because I cannot answer her question with identified evidence, I weigh the empirical gap more heavily in a first-place preference than I did in round 1. I leave vote prospects out of my reasoning and decide on the science and the attribution.

responses.point: Strömberg moved from B015 to B001 and argues that the award rests on the originating ideas, not on how well the estimated DSGE descendants forecast. He reads the post-2021 evidence as mixed and not as validation.
responses.response: I agree with this framing, and it settles how I treat the post-2021 episode. A prize for the originating ideas does not need the framework to have been validated by that episode, and I do not claim it was. I read the episode as a limit on the claim and not as a refutation, because the extensions it prompted (heterogeneity, state dependence) take the baseline framework as their reference. I disagree with him only on emphasis: the citation should not read as a certification of the baseline model's forecasting performance.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept origin of ideas as the criterion that separates Calvo, Taylor and Woodford from Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, or will want a laureate set that rewards estimation and quantification.
How the committee resolves priority questions involving Fischer, Phelps and Clarida, and whether the Taylor rule is treated as science or as policy prescription.
How much the mixed post-2021 and state-dependent pricing evidence should count against a citation centred on the originating ideas.
Whether my change of view is the correct judgement or reflects the weight of colleagues' arguments, which I have tried to separate from the support counts.
Whether B002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) should be preferred if the committee judges that B001 cannot be resolved into a defensible three-name attribution, and how the 2022 prize bears on it.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied files. I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or adoption figures.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure, not adjudicated. My supplied profile documents no collaboration with or tie to Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. My preferred part is now B001, and I co-authored the menu-costs and asymmetric price adjustment paper with committee colleague Richard Friberg and Tore Ellingsen, which is adjacent to the price-setting topics in B001. I am also a frequent co-author of committee colleagues Krusell and Boppart and an IIES colleague of both, and Krusell works on heterogeneous-agent macro, a successor literature to B001. None of them is a candidate. In round 1 I preferred B002, and none of its credited names is a documented tie of mine. My own research in dynamic macroeconomics, public finance and climate economics is adjacent to several shortlisted fields. I rely on the common criteria and record no recusal assumption.
